question.:question/problem: Which of the following lines is perpendicular to $-6x+9y=-13?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For the two lines to be perpendicular, their slopes must multiply to $-1.$

To find the slope of the given line $-6x+9y=-13,$ we convert to slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6x+9y & =-13 \\ 9y & =6x-13 \\ y & =\frac{6}{9}x-\frac{13}{9} \\ y & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{13}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

In slope-intercept form, the slope is the $x$-coefficient. So, the slope of the given line is $\frac{2}{3}.$

Looking at the answer choices, the line $y=-\frac{3}{2}x-3$ has a slope of $-\frac{3}{2}.$

Multiplying the slopes together, we have

$$
\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})=-1.
$$

Since the slopes multiply to $-1,$ we conclude that the line $y=-\frac{3}{2}x-3$ is perpendicular to the given line.
